title: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)
word: The gods and demons and the breath
hook: the gods audition every sense to sing their victory chant, and only the plain breath can't be corrupted
tomorrow: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the beginning there was nothing, and death covered it, and death was hungry. Your line was from hunger, the world. What did your own hunger build yesterday? Day three hundred sixty-two.

Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to the deathless. It's chanted in Sanskrit before classes, pujas, yoga sessions, school assemblies. And it comes from today's chapter of the Brihadaranyaka, at the end of a strange little war story. The gods and the demons, both children of the creator Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods have a plan: win with a chant. All they need is a singer the demons can't corrupt. So they start auditioning the parts of the body.
screen: `LEAD ME FROM THE UNREAL TO THE REAL.` → `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` → `THE GODS NEED A SINGER.`

segments.voice: First they ask speech. Speech sings for them, but keeps the best part for itself: the pleasure of speaking well. The demons notice, rush at it, and pierce it with evil. That, says the text, is why we say things we shouldn't. Then smell. Then the eye. Then the ear. Then the mind. Each one sings, each one keeps something back, each one gets pierced. That's why we see, hear and think things we wish we hadn't. Last, the gods turn to the breath in the mouth, the plain breath that keeps you alive. Breath sings. The demons rush at it too, and they shatter, the text says, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone. Why breath? One common reading: it took nothing for itself. It sang for everyone. A few weeks ago, the Chandogya told this same battle in a few lines, and its longer story had breath win by threatening to leave. Here the Brihadaranyaka tells the battle in full, and on this reading breath wins because it's the one faculty that doesn't grab. Then breath carries each of the others past death. Speech becomes fire. The eye becomes the sun. The ear becomes the directions. The mind becomes the moon. And the chapter ends with the chant: asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrityor ma amritam gamaya. The text explains its own words. The unreal is death; the real is the deathless. Darkness is death; light is the deathless. So this chant is, in its home, a prayer to be carried the way breath carries the senses.
screen: `SPEECH SINGS, AND KEEPS SOME FOR ITSELF.` · `EYE, EAR, MIND: EACH ONE PIERCED.` · `THE DEMONS SHATTER ON THE BREATH.` · `ASATO MA SAD GAMAYA.` · then, large: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one who sang. Sit, and let the breath move without steering it. Notice how it takes nothing for itself: it comes in, feeds every part of you, and goes. When a thought grabs you, a sound, a worry, a plan, let it be, and come back to the breath under it. If you pray, you can say the old chant silently on the out-breath: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless. The bell holds the time.
The gods and demons and the breath. In this story prana, the plain breath, is the one faculty the demons couldn't pierce, because it sang for everyone and kept nothing back.
screen: `THE GODS AND DEMONS AND THE BREATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breath is untouched by evil. Today, when you catch yourself about to say something you'll wish you hadn't, give it one breath first. Day three hundred sixty-two.

screen: `DAY 362 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "I AM" — THE SELF ALONE, AFRAID, THEN DESIRING.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus chant asato ma sad gamaya at the start of study, worship or a gathering, and teachers often explain its three lines as the movement from death to the deathless.

fork.setup: you're one of the gods. speech, smell, the eye, the ear and the mind have all sung, and the demons pierced every one. who do you ask next?
options: the mind again, louder this time.
the plain breath in the mouth.
give up and let the demons have the worlds.
fork.reveal: they ask the breath. it keeps nothing for itself, and the demons break on it like a clod of earth thrown against a stone.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, the life-force. pra (forth) + an (to breathe).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old myth about gods fighting demons.
what it means: every sense that grabs something for itself can be corrupted. the breath, which only gives, can't be.
what a scholar hears: the chant asato ma sad gamaya is glossed by the text itself (1.3.28): unreal and darkness mean death, real and light mean the deathless.

notes: The index word is the title's head cut mid-word ("The gods and demons and the breath"); kept exactly as the validator requires. Suggest the outline give this day a word such as prana.
Order of the senses in 1.3 (speech, smell/breath of the nose, eye, ear, mind) and that each kept the enjoyment for itself: summarized from 1.3.2–6; confirm.
Breath of the mouth named Ayasya Angirasa (1.3.8, 'essence of the limbs') was left out for length; the clod-against-stone image is 1.3.7.
Elements: speech to fire, nose-breath to wind, eye to sun, ear to the quarters, mind to moon (1.3.12–16); the script omits wind for brevity. Confirm.
The text's own gloss of the three lines (1.3.28) is paraphrased. Transliteration given without diacritics: asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya, mṛtyor mā'mṛtaṃ gamaya.

Reviewer edit: 'breath took nothing for itself' is an interpretation (the text contrasts the senses that kept the good part for themselves with the breath the demons could not pierce, 1.3.2–7), now framed as the usual reading; 'the most-sung prayer' softened to 'the best-known chant'.
Day 333 retold a senses-contest story under Chandogya 1.2; this script refers back to it only as 'the senses argued over who was greatest'.

Review (2026-10-01): hook no longer says listeners 'have no idea' of the chant's source; day 333 already told the Chandogya 1.2 version with the clod-against-stone image, so the teach now names it as the same battle rather than presenting it as new; word segment now speaks the index word (it said 'Prana', which mismatched the say-it games); 'best-known' superlatives cut.
